episodes.212526: A storm moving over Ortonville on the evening of June 4 produced large hail and strong winds. The Automated Weather Observing System at Ortonville municipal airport recorded a peak wind gust of 58 mph, while a resident adjacent to the airport property observed hail to the size of golf-balls. The storm produced additional quarter-sized hail as it continued eastward.
episodes.212568: Two distinct clusters of severe thunderstorms impacted central and northeast South Dakota during the afternoon and evening of June 4. In the northeast, severe storms generated large hail up to golf ball size five miles south-southeast of Cottonwood Lake and nine miles southeast of Tulare. The Huron Remote Automated Weather Station (RAWS) 12 miles east-southeast of Sunshine Bible Academy recorded a peak wind gust of 86 mph.||A separate cluster of storms tracked through mainly central and south central South Dakota producing peak wind gusts of 71 mph and 68 mph at the South Dakota Department of Transportation Road Weather Information System (RWIS) stations six miles southwest of the Joe Creek Recreation Area and nine miles north-northwest of Vivian, respectively.
episodes.212596: Scattered severe storms impacted north central and northeast Kansas on June 4th with wind damage including a short lived but strong tornado that developed over the community of Riley and moved northeast for approximately 4-5 miles.  It produced EF2 damage with winds to around 120 mph at one home just northeast of Riley.  No injuries were reported.
episodes.212856: Much of the day of the fifth was cloudy which prevented boundary layer mixing and thus inhibited most convection. Some clearing of clouds over eastern New Mexico into the western South Plains allowed rapid heating to occur which resulted in scattered thunderstorm activity. Weak atmospheric flow allowed storms to train over western Cochran County which produced heavy rainfall and flash flooding along Texas State Highway 114.
episodes.213269: A couple of different rounds of thunderstorms brought heavy rain to portions of the headwaters of the Big Sioux River. This heavy rain resulted in the upper portions of the Big Sioux rising above flood stage for a short period.
episodes.213271: A slow-moving upper low and increasing moisture content contributed to a period of active weather during the weekend of June 5, with scattered showers and thunderstorms occurring across the area mainly in the evening and overnight hours. Flash flooding was the primary weather hazard throughout the weekend, along with isolated instances of hail and damaging winds.
episodes.213599: A surface cold front bisected Minnesota which had produced thunderstorms during the pre-dawn hours of Friday, June 5th, 2026. A strong low-level jet which had supported this development weakened, thus allowing for gradual clearing and building instability during the daytime hours. A suitable environment for severe thunderstorms was realized across the eastern Dakotas and western Minnesota as precipitable water values exceeded 1 inch and dew points crept into the 60s.  Storms redeveloped that afternoon across western MN along this same stalled boundary and producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.
episodes.213744: Showers and thunderstorms affected the combined Panhandles each afternoon and evening in the early parts of June. With enough moisture, instability and sources to provide atmospheric lift, these storms were able to become severe each day and bring large hail to the region. A few instances of damaging winds and flooding also occurred.
episodes.213794: During the afternoon of the 4th, an upper-level trough was moving in from the west. Synoptic lift ahead of this feature, coupled with upslope flow and some lift from decaying outflow, allowed showers and thunderstorms to develop in/around the higher terrain and in western portions of the Permian Basin. Convection tended to move slowly and produce heavy rainfall during the evening and into the early morning hours of the 5th. As a result, flash flooding was reported in Gaines and Pecos Counties.
episodes.213796: A few hours after convection from the morning largely decayed, additional showers and thunderstorms developed thanks to an upper-level trough moving over west Texas and southeast New Mexico (along with upslope flow and some remnant outflow boundaries). Heavy rain led to flash flooding in Dawson County, while a landspout was observed west of Hobbs.
episodes.214097: Flash flooding occurred over the Houston metro area.
episodes.214110: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.
episodes.214113: During the early morning hours of June 5, 2026, thunderstorms producing heavy rainfall triggered flash flooding across southern Richardson County. Consecutive rounds of thunderstorms generated intense rainfall rates of 1.50 to 3.00 inches per hour, driving estimated total rainfall to between 4.00 and 6.00 inches. Falls City Brenner Field Airport measured a storm total of 4.84 inches. Delayed reports received later in the day from Emergency Management and Law Enforcement indicated flash flooding over several roads, including 635 Avenue, 706 Trail, 656 Avenue, Fulton Street near Highway 73 south of Falls City, and 704 Road near Highways 73 and 159.
episodes.214342: A slow-moving upper low across southwest Texas provided for several days of thunderstorm activity across Oklahoma and western-north Texas, the first of which occurred on the 5th. A few stronger multi-cell thunderstorms produced damaging downburst winds in the afternoon and early evening.
episodes.214343: A slow-moving upper low across southwest Texas provided for several days of thunderstorm activity across Oklahoma and western-north Texas, the first of which occurred on the 5th. A few stronger multi-cell thunderstorms produced damaging downburst winds in the afternoon and early evening.
episodes.214520: A cold front moved across the Upper Midwest on the 5th and led to the development of a few thunderstorms as it passed. One of the storms was stronger than most and led to some isolated wind damage in Pine County.
episodes.214564: A low pressure system passing north of Lake Superior brought scattered showers and thunderstorms to Michigan's Upper Peninsula on the 5th, with one storm bringing 1 inch hail to Marquette County.
episodes.214601: Leftover boundaries from June 3 thunderstorms and diurnally driven MLCAPE up to 1500-2000 J/kg triggered rapid storm development in the mid-James River Valley by mid-to-late afternoon. These storms intensified due to 40-45 kts of effective shear, producing hail as large as baseballs.
episodes.214958: A cluster of thunderstorms developed over the Pine Ridge of northwestern Nebraska during the early evening hours of June 4th. As this activity pushed east into Sheridan and Cherry Counties, it strengthened, becoming severe. Severe storms tracked east across northern Cherry County before weakening over Keya Paha, northern Brown and northern Rock Counties. Hail up to quarter size and thunderstorm wind gusts up to 72 MPH were reported with the strongest storms.
episodes.215001: A few strong to severe thunderstorms produced low end severe weather across the Black Hills.
episodes.215088: An upper-level low moved across Texas where a warm, moist airmass was in place. This disturbance generated thunderstorms. Some of these storms produced locally heavy rain that led to flash flooding.
episodes.215472: Scattered thunderstorms produced isolated large hail and localized flash flooding across the eastern half of the area.
episodes.215739: The afternoon sea breeze, combined with a weak upper level disturbance approaching the Lower Texas Coast, triggered two bands of slow-moving thunderstorms that dropped more than 3 of rainfall in a short period of time.  One band, across the west half of Brownsville, created localized flash flooding with water between 2 and 3 feet in some areas. A second band across the sand flats between SR 48 and SR 100 (south of Los Fresnos) dropped an estimated 5+ of rainfall - but no significant flooding was reported, even in Los Fresnos, where more than 3 fell.
episodes.216027: The combination of a departing mid latitude upper trough, a lingering upper trough to the southwest of the Florida Keys, little or no convective inhibition and precipitation water above 2.1 inches resulted in concentrated heavy convective rainfall within the city of Key West.
episodes.216028: A lightning strike damaging a vessel was reported in the Key West Anchorage, with isolated marine thunderstorm wind gusts reported oceanside of the Lower Florida Keys.

During the early morning hours of June 5, 2026, thunderstorms producing heavy rainfall triggered flash flooding across southern Richardson County. Consecutive rounds of thunderstorms generated intense rainfall rates of 1.50 to 3.00 inches per hour, driving estimated total rainfall to between 4.00 and 6.00 inches. As a result, the Big Nemaha River gauge at Falls City (FLLN1) rose above flood stage at 2:45 AM CST on June 5th. The gauge crested at 31.09 ft, consistent with moderate flooding, at 11:28 AM CST on June 5th. The gauge fell below flood stage at 2:45 AM CST on June 6th.
